subject: Ophthalmology
q: Which is the earliest symptom of retinitis pigmentosa?
why: Central vision loss is a late feature
Metamorphopsia suggests macular pathology, not RP
Correct — earliest feature from rod dysfunction
Diplopia is not a feature of RP
exp: Nyctalopia is the earliest symptom of retinitis pigmentosa because rod photoreceptors in the mid-periphery degenerate first, followed by progressive field constriction (ring scotoma to tunnel vision) with only late central vision loss; fundus shows bone-spicule pigmentation and attenuated vessels.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Timolol lowers intraocular pressure mainly by which mechanism?
opts: Producing miosis to widen the angle
why: Uveoscleral outflow is increased by prostaglandin analogues, not timolol
Trabecular outflow is enhanced by miotics
Miosis is produced by pilocarpine-type drugs
Correct — reduces aqueous production via ciliary beta-2 blockade
exp: Topical beta-blockers like timolol block beta-2 receptors on the ciliary epithelium, reducing aqueous humor production, in contrast to prostaglandin analogues which increase uveoscleral outflow and are now preferred first-line.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: The Fleischer ring seen in keratoconus is composed of deposits of which substance?
why: Correct — iron deposition in the corneal epithelium
Calcium deposition describes band keratopathy
Copper deposition describes the Kayser-Fleischer ring of Wilson disease
Melanin is not the basis of the Fleischer ring
exp: The Fleischer ring is iron deposition in the corneal epithelium at the base of the ectatic cone, best seen with a cobalt-blue filter, distinct from Munson's sign and Vogt's striae, the other classic keratoconus signs.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A pupil that accommodates normally but fails to react to light (light-near dissociation) is characteristic of which condition?
why: Adie's pupil is tonic and slowly reactive in young women, unrelated to syphilis
Correct — light-near dissociation of neurosyphilis
Horner syndrome causes miosis with ptosis and anhidrosis, not light-near dissociation
Marcus Gunn pupil shows paradoxical dilation on the swinging-light test, not light-near dissociation
exp: The Argyll Robertson pupil is a classic sign of neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis), from a lesion disrupting the light-reflex pathway near the Edinger-Westphal nucleus while sparing the near-reflex pathway; it is bilateral, small and irregular.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: The Jackson cross-cylinder is an optical instrument used mainly to:
opts: Measure the axial length of the eye
Refine the axis and power of astigmatic correction during subjective refraction
why: Axial length is measured by biometry, not the cross-cylinder
IOP is measured by tonometry
Correct — refines cylindrical axis/power during subjective refraction
Corneal curvature is measured by keratometry
exp: The Jackson cross-cylinder combines equal plus and minus cylindrical power at right angles and is flipped in front of a patient's trial correction to fine-tune the axis and power of astigmatism during subjective refraction.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Snowbanking over the pars plana with vitreous 'snowball' opacities is characteristic of which condition?
why: Anterior uveitis shows KPs and anterior chamber flare, not snowbanking
Posterior scleritis causes pain and choroidal folds, not vitreous snowballs
Toxocara produces a focal granuloma in a child, not classic snowbanking
Correct — defining feature of pars planitis
exp: Pars planitis is idiopathic intermediate uveitis in young adults, characterized by vitreous snowballs and inferior snowbanking; it can be associated with multiple sclerosis, and its main complications are cystoid macular edema and vitreous hemorrhage.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Branch retinal vein occlusion typically occurs at which site?
opts: An arteriovenous crossing where a thickened artery compresses the vein
why: Correct — classic arteriovenous-crossing pathogenesis
Disc cupping is a glaucoma finding
Photoreceptor degeneration describes RP/AMD, not BRVO
Vitreous base traction is implicated in retinal tears, not venous occlusion
exp: BRVO characteristically occurs at an arteriovenous crossing where a thickened, sclerotic arteriole sharing a common adventitial sheath compresses the vein, producing a sectoral area of hemorrhage and edema; risk factors mirror CRVO but the visual prognosis is generally better.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: In a patient with a red eye and mild discomfort, instillation of topical phenylephrine causes blanching of the injected vessels. This finding suggests:
why: Correct — superficial episcleral vessels blanch with phenylephrine, distinguishing episcleritis from scleritis.
Scleral vessels do not blanch with phenylephrine because the deeper episcleral/scleral plexus is involved.
Angle closure presents with a fixed mid-dilated pupil, severe pain, and corneal edema, unrelated to this test.
Uveitis shows ciliary flush and is not characterized by this blanching test.
exp: The phenylephrine blanching test distinguishes episcleritis (superficial vessels blanch, generally benign and self-limiting) from scleritis (deeper vessels do not blanch and inflammation is more fixed, often linked to systemic autoimmune disease requiring workup and treatment).

subject: Ophthalmology
q: The unit used to measure the angle of ocular deviation in strabismus, defined as 1 cm of light-ray displacement at 1 meter distance, is called:
why: The dioptre measures refractive/lens power (reciprocal of focal length in metres), not deviation angle.
Correct — the prism diopter measures gaze deviation in strabismus with this exact definition.
The Snellen fraction measures visual acuity.
The Hess screen is a chart/test for ocular motility, not itself a unit of measurement.
exp: The prism diopter (delta) measures gaze deviation in strabismus, where 1 delta equals 1 cm of displacement at 1 m; it is used with the prism bar cover test to quantify squint angle for surgical planning.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 40-year-old woman presents with bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with mutton-fat keratic precipitates and iris nodules; chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and serum ACE is elevated. Diagnosis?
why: Tuberculous uveitis can also be granulomatous, but bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with elevated ACE is far more specific for sarcoidosis.
Toxoplasma causes focal necrotizing retinochoroiditis (headlight in the fog), not a granulomatous panuveitis with hilar nodes.
Correct — ocular sarcoidosis presents with this bilateral granulomatous panuveitis, elevated ACE, and hilar lymphadenopathy.
Behcet's disease causes non-granulomatous panuveitis with hypopyon, alongside oral and genital ulcers, not hilar lymphadenopathy.
exp: Ocular sarcoidosis presents as bilateral granulomatous uveitis with mutton-fat keratic precipitates and iris (Koeppe/Busacca) nodules, associated with elevated serum ACE and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray; treatment is directed at the underlying sarcoidosis with systemic corticosteroids.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A tall, thin child with fair hair, learning difficulty, and a history of thromboembolic events is found to have bilateral inferonasal lens dislocation. Likely diagnosis?
why: Marfan syndrome causes superotemporal lens dislocation with normal intelligence and no thromboembolic tendency.
Weill-Marchesani syndrome causes microspherophakia with lens dislocation, but patients are short with brachydactyly, not tall.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome causes joint hypermobility and skin hyperextensibility, not classic lens dislocation.
Correct — homocystinuria causes inferonasal lens dislocation with marfanoid habitus, learning difficulty, and thromboembolism.
exp: Homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) causes inferonasal lens dislocation from zonular weakness - the opposite direction to Marfan's superotemporal dislocation - and is associated with a marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability, and thromboembolism from elevated homocysteine, key features that distinguish it from Marfan syndrome.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 3-month-old infant presents with excessive tearing, photophobia, blepharospasm, and enlarged, hazy corneas (buphthalmos). Diagnosis and characteristic corneal finding?
why: Correct — this triad with buphthalmos and Haab's striae is classic for primary congenital glaucoma.
Brushfield spots are iris findings seen in Down syndrome, unrelated to congenital cataract or this presentation.
ROP occurs in premature infants with abnormal retinal vascularization, not corneal enlargement and tearing.
Salt-and-pepper retinopathy is a retinal, not corneal, finding of congenital rubella.
exp: Primary congenital glaucoma presents with the classic triad of epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm, with buphthalmos from raised intraocular pressure in the distensible infant eye; Haab's striae are horizontal or curvilinear breaks in Descemet's membrane, and urgent surgical management (goniotomy or trabeculotomy) is required.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A patient three months after penetrating keratoplasty presents with redness, pain, and decreased vision; slit-lamp examination shows a line of keratic precipitates advancing across the corneal endothelium with graft edema. This finding is called:
why: The Kayser-Fleischer ring is copper deposition in Descemet's membrane in Wilson's disease, unrelated to graft rejection.
Correct — the Khodadoust line marks endothelial graft rejection, the most serious rejection type.
Vogt's striae are vertical stress lines seen in keratoconus.
The Fleischer ring is iron deposition at the base of the cone in keratoconus.
exp: The Khodadoust line is an endothelial graft-rejection line - inflammatory keratic precipitates progressing across the donor corneal endothelium - marking endothelial rejection, the most serious rejection type since the endothelium does not regenerate; urgent intensive topical or systemic corticosteroids are needed to try to salvage the graft.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Which investigation is used to monitor visual field loss and progression in a patient with glaucoma?
why: Assesses the anterior chamber angle to classify open- vs closed-angle glaucoma, not to monitor field progression.
Measures central corneal thickness, which affects IOP interpretation, not field monitoring.
Correct - automated static perimetry quantifies and tracks glaucomatous field defects over serial visits.
Measures axial length, mainly for IOL power calculation before cataract surgery, unrelated to glaucoma monitoring.
exp: Automated static perimetry (e.g., Humphrey visual field analyzer) quantifies and tracks the characteristic visual field defects of glaucoma - such as arcuate scotomas and a nasal step - over serial visits, making it the standard tool for monitoring functional progression.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A well-defined grey-white ring is seen at the corneal periphery, separated from the limbus by a clear zone, in an asymptomatic 75-year-old. What is this finding, and when does the identical finding become clinically significant?
opts: Kayser-Fleischer ring; significant only if the patient is elderly
Arcus juvenilis; always pathological regardless of age
Arcus senilis; a benign aging change, but significant (suggesting dyslipidemia) if seen under age 40
why: The Kayser-Fleischer ring is classically brown/greenish, sits in Descemet's membrane, and occurs in young patients with liver/neuropsychiatric disease.
Band keratopathy is a horizontal calcium deposit across the interpalpebral cornea, a different appearance, linked to chronic uveitis/hypercalcemia.
Arcus in a young patient warrants a lipid workup but is not itself invariably pathological.
Correct - arcus senilis is benign in the elderly but should prompt a lipid profile if seen before age 40.
exp: Arcus senilis is a common, benign, age-related peripheral corneal lipid deposit with no visual or systemic significance in the elderly; the identical-looking ring in a patient under 40 ('arcus juvenilis') should prompt a lipid profile, as it can indicate a familial hyperlipidemia.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Blue sclera is a classic clinical feature of which connective tissue disorder?
why: Correct - defective type I collagen causes scleral thinning, letting the underlying uvea show through.
Its ocular hallmark is superotemporal lens subluxation, not blue sclera.
Associated with skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility and vascular fragility, not classically blue sclera.
Causes downward lens dislocation and a marfanoid habitus, again not blue sclera.
exp: In osteogenesis imperfecta, defective type I collagen causes scleral thinning, allowing the underlying uveal pigment to show through and give a characteristic blue tinge, alongside bone fragility/fractures and sometimes hearing loss.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Superotemporal (upward) dislocation of the lens is classically associated with which condition, distinguishing it from the downward dislocation seen in homocystinuria?
why: Causes anterior lenticonus and a perimacular retinal fleck pattern, not zonular dislocation.
Correct - a fibrillin-1 defect weakens zonules asymmetrically, subluxing the lens upward and outward.
Associated with the Kayser-Fleischer ring and sunflower cataract, not lens dislocation.
Causes ipsilateral glaucoma and choroidal hemangioma, not lens ectopia.
exp: In Marfan syndrome, a fibrillin-1 defect weakens the zonular fibers asymmetrically, causing the lens to sublux upward and outward (superotemporally); in homocystinuria the lens typically displaces inferonasally (downward) - a classic distinguishing exam point.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A young adult has chronic, mild, unilateral anterior uveitis with fine stellate keratic precipitates, heterochromia (the affected iris is lighter), and no posterior synechiae, but later develops cataract and glaucoma. What is the diagnosis?
why: Typically acute, recurrent, unilateral-alternating and painful, with posterior synechiae and hypopyon in severe cases.
Causes recurrent, severe, often bilateral panuveitis with hypopyon and retinal vasculitis, not this mild indolent picture.
Correct - fine stellate KPs, heterochromia and no posterior synechiae are classic for Fuchs iridocyclitis.
Bilateral granulomatous uveitis following penetrating trauma to one eye, not this unilateral spontaneous presentation.
exp: Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a chronic, typically unilateral, low-grade anterior uveitis marked by fine stellate keratic precipitates and iris heterochromia, distinctively without posterior synechiae despite chronic inflammation; it commonly leads to secondary cataract and glaucoma over time.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 55-year-old myopic patient reports sudden flashes of light followed by floaters and a curtain-like shadow progressing across the visual field. What is the underlying mechanism?
opts: Occlusion of the central retinal artery
Leakage of fluid from a choroidal neovascular membrane
Ischemia of the retinal capillary bed from microvascular disease
Retinal tear following posterior vitreous detachment, allowing fluid to separate the neurosensory retina
why: CRAO causes sudden painless profound monocular vision loss with a cherry-red spot, not a progressive curtain with preceding flashes/floaters.
Wet AMD causes distortion/metamorphopsia and gradual central vision loss, not this acute peripheral-to-central curtain.
Diabetic/hypertensive ischemia causes gradual vision changes with cotton-wool spots/hemorrhages, not sudden flashes-floaters-curtain.
Correct - posterior vitreous detachment tearing the retina, with fluid tracking beneath it, is rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
exp: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment begins with posterior vitreous detachment, which can tear the retina at areas of vitreoretinal adhesion; liquefied vitreous then tracks through the tear beneath the neurosensory retina, producing the classic flashes-floaters-then-curtain field loss - an ophthalmic emergency requiring urgent surgical repair.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Retinal hemorrhages with pale, white centers on fundus examination are classically associated with which condition?
why: Roth spots are the classic retinal sign of IE, from septic microemboli or immune-complex vasculitis
Diabetic retinopathy shows dot-blot/flame hemorrhages without the characteristic white center
CRVO gives diffuse blood-and-thunder hemorrhages, not discrete white-centered spots
Hypertensive retinopathy shows flame hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots, not Roth spots specifically
exp: Roth spots (retinal hemorrhage with a white/pale fibrin-platelet center) classically indicate infective endocarditis, but also occur in severe anemia, leukemia, and diabetes - always correlate with fever, murmur, and blood cultures.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: First-line topical prostaglandin analogues (e.g. latanoprost) lower intraocular pressure by which mechanism?
opts: Constricting the pupil to open the trabecular meshwork
Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body
why: This describes beta-blockers (timolol), not prostaglandin analogues
This describes miotics (pilocarpine)
This describes carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide/dorzolamide)
Prostaglandin analogues increase uveoscleral outflow, the correct mechanism
exp: Prostaglandin analogues are first-line for POAG because they increase uveoscleral (non-conventional) outflow with once-daily dosing and minimal systemic side effects, unlike aqueous-suppressant classes.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A V-shaped indentation of the lower eyelid margin on downgaze in a patient with progressive corneal thinning is known as?
why: Fleischer ring is an iron deposition ring at the base of the cone, not a lid sign
Vogt's striae are fine stromal stress lines seen on slit-lamp, not a lid contour sign
Munson's sign is correctly the lid-contour sign of advanced keratoconus
Scissoring is a retinoscopy reflex finding, not a lid sign
exp: Munson's sign is a clinical sign of advanced keratoconus - the conical cornea tents the lower lid on downgaze - distinct from Fleischer ring (iron deposit at the cone base) and Vogt's striae (fine vertical stress lines in the deep stroma), which are slit-lamp signs of the same disease.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 24-year-old woman develops sudden painful loss of vision and impaired color perception in the right eye; swinging a light from the left eye to the right causes the right pupil to paradoxically dilate. Which finding and diagnosis best fit?
opts: Relative afferent pupillary defect from optic neuritis
why: Horner syndrome gives miosis with ptosis, not an afferent pupillary defect
RAPD plus painful vision loss and color desaturation correctly indicates optic neuritis
Argyll Robertson pupil accommodates but doesn't react to light, seen in neurosyphilis, not this picture
Papilledema is bilateral disc swelling from raised ICP, not a unilateral painful vision loss with RAPD
exp: Painful monocular vision loss with dyschromatopsia and a positive swinging-flashlight test (Marcus Gunn pupil) is the classic triad of optic neuritis, often the first presentation of multiple sclerosis - order an MRI brain/orbits with contrast.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: During streak retinoscopy performed at a 50 cm working distance on a 6-year-old child, a with movement is neutralized using a +2.00 D lens. After correcting for the working-distance factor, what is the child's actual refractive error?
why: Subtracting the 2 D working-distance factor from the 2 D neutralizing lens correctly gives plano
This would be true only if the working-distance factor were ignored
This reverses the sign incorrectly
This doubles the neutralizing power instead of subtracting the working-distance factor
exp: The working-distance lens (reciprocal of distance in metres) must always be subtracted from the neutralizing power to get true refractive error; at 50 cm this factor is +2.00 D, so +2.00 D neutralizing power minus 2.00 D working-distance factor equals plano.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 35-year-old presents with bilateral blurred vision, headache, and tinnitus, followed weeks later by patchy whitening of the hair and eyelashes; fundus examination shows bilateral exudative retinal detachments with a sunset-glow appearance. What is the diagnosis?
why: Sympathetic ophthalmia follows penetrating trauma/surgery to the fellow eye, with no auditory or skin findings
Behcet gives hypopyon uveitis with oral/genital ulcers, not poliosis or tinnitus
Sarcoid uveitis shows mutton-fat KPs and systemic granulomas, not this triad
VKH's neuro-oculo-cutaneous syndrome correctly fits this full picture
exp: VKH is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis targeting melanocytes, with meningeal (headache), auditory (tinnitus), and integumentary (poliosis, vitiligo, alopecia) involvement; the late sunset-glow fundus reflects choroidal melanocyte destruction.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A cup-disc ratio of 0.7 with an inter-eye asymmetry of 0.3, in a patient with a normal intraocular pressure of 16 mmHg, is most suggestive of which condition?
why: Correct - cupping/asymmetry/field loss with normal IOP is classic normal-tension glaucoma
Physiological cupping is usually symmetric with no field defect and rarely this high a ratio
Disc drusen mimics disc swelling (pseudopapilledema), not cupping
Papilledema shows a swollen, blurred disc margin with raised ICP signs, not increased cupping
exp: Normal-tension glaucoma is glaucomatous optic neuropathy (pathological cupping, inter-eye asymmetry, field loss) occurring despite statistically normal IOP; it is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out diurnal IOP variation and congenital disc anomalies.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 5-year-old girl with oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis and ANA positivity requires periodic ophthalmologic screening for asymptomatic anterior uveitis. What is the recommended screening interval?
opts: Only if the child develops visual symptoms
Once at the time of diagnosis only
Every 12 months regardless of risk category
why: Symptom-triggered screening misses silent uveitis, which is often asymptomatic in this group.
A one-time screen at diagnosis does not cover the ongoing multi-year risk.
Annual screening applies to lower-risk categories, not the high-risk group.
Correct - high-risk JIA subtypes (young-onset, ANA-positive, oligoarticular) require frequent screening, commonly every 3 months.
exp: JIA-associated anterior uveitis is frequently asymptomatic, especially in young-onset ANA-positive oligoarticular disease, so high-risk children need frequent slit-lamp screening to catch uveitis before band keratopathy, synechiae, or glaucoma develop; screening interval is risk-stratified and periodically revised in consensus guidelines.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: During accommodation for near vision, the crystalline lens becomes more convex due to:
opts: Relaxation of ciliary muscle increasing zonular tension
Contraction of ciliary muscle relaxing zonular tension
why: This is the opposite - ciliary relaxation increases zonular tension and flattens the lens for distance
Correct - ciliary contraction slackens zonules allowing the lens to become more spherical
Pupillary constriction is part of the near triad but does not itself change lens shape
Lateral rectus governs eye abduction and is unrelated to accommodation
exp: Accommodation: the ciliary muscle contracts, slackening the zonular fibers, allowing the lens to assume a more spherical, convex shape by its own elasticity, increasing refractive power for near objects.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 58-year-old woman presents with sudden severe unilateral eye pain, blurred vision, halos around lights, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil with a hard eyeball on palpation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: POAG is typically painless and slowly progressive, not this acute picture
Correct - sudden pain, halos, fixed mid-dilated pupil, and raised IOP mark acute angle-closure glaucoma
Anterior uveitis causes a constricted (not dilated) pupil with circumcorneal congestion
Conjunctivitis does not cause severe pain, halos, or raised IOP
exp: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency presenting with sudden severe pain, halos, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, corneal haze, and markedly raised IOP - immediate IOP-lowering therapy is followed by laser peripheral iridotomy.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Hypopyon (a layered collection of white cells in the anterior chamber) in a young patient with recurrent oral and genital ulcers is most characteristic of which condition?
why: Fuchs is mild and non-granulomatous, and does NOT cause hypopyon or posterior synechiae
Sarcoid uveitis is typically granulomatous with mutton-fat KPs, not classically hypopyon-forming
Correct
HLA-B27 uveitis is recurrent and non-granulomatous but lacks the oral/genital ulcer association and hypopyon is less classic
exp: Hypopyon uveitis is a hallmark of Behcet disease, a systemic vasculitis with recurrent oral/genital ulcers, skin lesions (erythema nodosum, pathergy), and potentially blinding panuveitis/retinal vasculitis treated with systemic immunosuppression.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A rapidly progressive corneal ulcer with a ground-glass, greenish-yellow stromal infiltrate and copious mucopurulent discharge in a soft contact lens wearer is most typically caused by which organism?
why: S. aureus causes a more indolent, round/oval ulcer with grayish-white infiltrate
S. pneumoniae causes a serpiginous ulcer with hypopyon following trauma, not linked to contact lens wear
Fusarium is a fungal keratitis pathogen linked to vegetable-matter trauma, with a dry feathery infiltrate
Correct — Pseudomonas is strongly associated with contact lens wear and rapid stromal melting
exp: Pseudomonas aeruginosa keratitis is strongly associated with soft contact lens wear (biofilm on lens/case) and is notorious for rapid, aggressive stromal melting with a characteristic greenish-yellow, ground-glass infiltrate — a sight-threatening emergency requiring fortified topical aminoglycoside/fluoroquinolone therapy.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Necrotizing scleritis, the most severe and vision-threatening form of scleral inflammation, is most commonly associated with which systemic autoimmune disease?
why: Correct — RA is the commonest systemic association of necrotizing scleritis
SLE can cause scleritis but is a less common association for the necrotizing form
Sarcoidosis more classically causes granulomatous uveitis
Ankylosing spondylitis is classically linked to acute anterior uveitis (HLA-B27), not necrotizing scleritis
exp: Rheumatoid arthritis is the systemic disease most frequently underlying necrotizing scleritis, which can progress to scleromalacia perforans and carries significant risk of globe perforation and vision loss — it signals severe, often erosive systemic RA and merits systemic immunosuppression.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: The hallmark feature that distinguishes proliferative from non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy is:
why: Microaneurysms are an early feature present in both stages
Hard exudates occur in both stages, not the discriminator
Dot-blot hemorrhages are an NPDR feature
Correct - neovascularization defines the proliferative stage
exp: The transition from non-proliferative to proliferative diabetic retinopathy is defined by the appearance of retinal or disc neovascularization driven by VEGF in response to retinal ischemia - this is the trigger for anti-VEGF therapy or panretinal photocoagulation to prevent vitreous hemorrhage and tractional detachment.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: The feature that distinguishes pterygium from pinguecula is that pterygium:
opts: Extension across the limbus onto the cornea
Yellowish-white elevation lateral to the limbus without corneal extension
Subepithelial elastotic degeneration confined to the conjunctiva
why: Correct - pterygium invades across the limbus onto the cornea, unlike pinguecula
This describes pinguecula's own appearance, not the discriminating feature
Elastotic degeneration on histology is shared by both lesions
Chronic UV exposure is a shared risk factor for both lesions, not a discriminator
exp: The defining distinction is anatomic: pterygium is a triangular fibrovascular conjunctival growth that actually invades across the limbus onto the cornea (risking astigmatism or visual axis involvement if it progresses), while pinguecula stays confined to the bulbar conjunctiva without crossing onto the cornea.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 70-year-old man reports gradually progressive blurring of central vision over 2 years. Fundus examination shows multiple discrete yellowish deposits at the posterior pole with areas of retinal pigment epithelium mottling; OCT shows no intraretinal or subretinal fluid. The most likely diagnosis is:
why: Correct — gradual painless central vision loss with drusen/RPE mottling and no fluid on OCT is classic dry AMD
Wet AMD is defined by choroidal neovascularisation with subretinal/intraretinal fluid or haemorrhage on OCT, absent here
Central serous chorioretinopathy typically affects younger men with a neurosensory detachment and subretinal fluid, not drusen
Vitelliform dystrophy shows a characteristic yellow egg-yolk macular lesion, usually presenting earlier in life, not drusen with RPE mottling
exp: Dry (non-exudative) AMD is characterised by drusen (extracellular deposits between the RPE and Bruch's membrane) and gradual RPE atrophy/mottling, progressing slowly without neovascularisation or fluid on OCT; wet AMD involves choroidal neovascularisation with subretinal/intraretinal fluid or haemorrhage and is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF agents.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: The duochrome (bichrome) test used at the end of subjective refraction relies on which principle to fine-tune the refractive endpoint?
why: Correct, exploits chromatic aberration where red focuses slightly behind and green slightly in front of the retina in emmetropia
Purkinje shift is the scotopic-photopic sensitivity peak shift, unrelated
Stiles-Crawford effect concerns directional sensitivity of foveal cones, unrelated
Scheiner's principle underlies optometers/retinoscopy doubling, not this test
exp: The duochrome test is a quick, patient-friendly endpoint check - if letters look clearer on the red background the patient is under-corrected, clearer on green means over-corrected - a frequently tested optics application.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A contact lens wearer presents with a painful corneal ulcer, pain out of proportion to clinical signs, and a ring-shaped stromal infiltrate that has failed to respond to broad-spectrum antibiotics. What is the most likely causative organism?
why: Pseudomonas causes a rapidly progressive, more purulent ulcer but usually responds at least partially to antibiotics and doesn't classically show a ring infiltrate
Correct, contact-lens-associated ring infiltrate with disproportionate pain and antibiotic non-response
S. aureus causes a more localized, less painful ulcer
HSV causes a dendritic ulcer with reduced corneal sensation, not a ring infiltrate
exp: Acanthamoeba keratitis should be suspected in any contact lens wearer with a non-healing, antibiotic-resistant ulcer with severe pain out of proportion to findings - diagnosis is by corneal scraping (cysts on KOH/calcofluor white stain) or confocal microscopy.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: What is the minimum reported latent period between penetrating ocular trauma and onset of sympathetic ophthalmia in the fellow (sympathizing) eye?
opts: It occurs simultaneously with the injury
why: Wrong — far too short; autoimmune sensitization takes longer than 24 hours.
Wrong — while some cases are delayed by months to years, the minimum reported latency is much shorter.
Wrong — sympathetic ophthalmia is by definition a delayed immune response, never simultaneous.
Correct — accepted minimum latency is about 2 weeks, underlying the 10-14 day teaching for prophylactic enucleation.
exp: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare bilateral granulomatous panuveitis following penetrating trauma (or intraocular surgery) to one eye, triggering an autoimmune attack on the fellow eye. The accepted minimum latent period is roughly 2 weeks (most cases occur within 3 months, rare cases delayed by years) — underlying the practice of considering prophylactic enucleation of a severely injured, blind eye within the first 10-14 days.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a chronic, typically unilateral, low-grade anterior uveitis. Which finding characteristically distinguishes it from other anterior uveitides?
opts: Marked pain, photophobia, and posterior synechiae
Hypopyon with a severe fibrinous reaction
Broad-based posterior synechiae causing iris bombe
Iris heterochromia with fine stellate keratic precipitates and notably absent posterior synechiae
why: Wrong — Fuchs is characteristically mild and painless, not marked pain and photophobia, and does not cause posterior synechiae.
Wrong — hypopyon and a fibrinous reaction suggest a more severe, acute uveitis (e.g. HLA-B27-associated), not the mild chronic Fuchs picture.
Wrong — posterior synechiae/iris bombe is specifically absent in Fuchs, a key distinguishing negative feature.
Correct — heterochromia, stellate KPs, and absent posterior synechiae are the hallmark distinguishing features.
exp: Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is characteristically a mild or even asymptomatic chronic anterior uveitis, with iris heterochromia (affected eye paler from stromal atrophy), fine stellate keratic precipitates scattered diffusely over the whole endothelium, and notably no posterior synechiae — a key discriminating feature. Associated with cataract and secondary glaucoma; fine abnormal iris vessels can cause hyphema after minor trauma (Amsler's sign).

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Image described: fundus photograph showing a fluffy yellow-white focal retinochoroiditis lesion with overlying vitreous haze, adjacent to an old pigmented chorioretinal scar, the headlight in fog appearance. Which organism classically causes this posterior uveitis picture?
why: CMV retinitis shows a pizza-pie or haemorrhagic granular pattern, not headlight-in-fog.
Tuberculous uveitis shows choroidal tubercles or serpiginous-like choroiditis, not this specific sign.
Correct — Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis is the classic cause of the headlight-in-fog appearance adjacent to an old scar.
Toxocara causes an eosinophilic peripheral retinal granuloma, typically in children with pica, not this sign.
exp: Toxoplasma gondii is the classic cause of posterior uveitis or retinochoroiditis, producing a focal fluffy white-yellow lesion with overlying vitritis, the headlight in fog sign, typically at the edge of an old pigmented scar from prior often congenital infection, since reactivation occurs at the scar margin. This distinguishes it from CMV retinitis, important in HIV-positive patients.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex) noticed in a 1-year-old must be urgently evaluated to rule out which sight- and life-threatening diagnosis?
why: Congenital cataract is a common benign cause of leukocoria but is not the life-threatening diagnosis that must be excluded first
Persistent fetal vasculature is a rarer structural cause of leukocoria, not the priority to rule out
Correct — retinoblastoma is the malignant cause of leukocoria that mandates urgent exclusion
A large chorioretinal coloboma can rarely cause leukocoria but is not the diagnosis of greatest urgency
exp: Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood and the most important cause of leukocoria to exclude urgently, since delayed diagnosis risks extraocular spread and death; though congenital cataract is a more frequent overall cause of leukocoria, retinoblastoma is the one that cannot be missed.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Which structure of the eye contributes the greatest proportion of its total refractive power?
why: The lens contributes real but smaller fixed power (about +20 D) plus variable accommodative power
Aqueous humor has minimal refractive power, mainly a fluid medium
correct — the air-cornea interface provides the single largest refractive jump, about two-thirds of total power
Vitreous humor is optically inert, contributing negligible refractive power
exp: The cornea contributes roughly two-thirds (about +43 D) of the eye's total refractive power (approximately +60 D), because the largest change in refractive index along the visual axis occurs at the air-tear film-cornea interface. The crystalline lens contributes the remaining fixed power plus the variable component needed for accommodation, but its total contribution is smaller than the cornea's.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 28-year-old man with chronic low backache and morning stiffness presents with sudden onset of a painful, red, photophobic right eye with blurred vision. Examination shows circumcorneal congestion and fine keratic precipitates without synechiae. This is his third such episode, each lasting about 6 weeks in the same eye and resolving completely. What is the most likely underlying association?
why: Sarcoidosis causes granulomatous uveitis with mutton-fat KPs and broad synechiae, usually more insidious and often bilateral.
Correct — acute, recurrent, non-granulomatous anterior uveitis with axial spondyloarthritis features fits HLA-B27 disease.
JIA-associated uveitis is typically chronic and asymptomatic ("white eye"), affecting young ANA-positive girls, unlike this acute painful presentation.
TB causes granulomatous uveitis with mutton-fat KPs and broad synechiae, a more chronic picture than described here.
exp: HLA-B27-associated acute anterior uveitis is classically unilateral, acute-onset, painful, recurrent (often alternating eyes), non-granulomatous (fine KPs, no broad synechiae initially), and self-limiting over weeks — seen with ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, IBD, and psoriatic arthritis.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A greenish-brown ring at the periphery of the corneal Descemet's membrane, best seen on slit-lamp examination, is characteristic of which systemic disease?
why: Hemochromatosis deposits iron in liver, pancreas, skin, and joints, not a corneal ring
Marfan syndrome causes lens subluxation and other ocular findings, not a corneal copper ring
Diabetes causes various corneal changes but not a Kayser-Fleischer ring
Correct — copper deposition in Descemet's membrane is the classic finding of Wilson disease
exp: The Kayser-Fleischer ring is copper deposition in the peripheral Descemet's membrane, seen in Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration from ATP7B mutation and impaired biliary copper excretion) — a key diagnostic clue alongside neuropsychiatric features and low serum ceruloplasmin.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A preterm infant born at 28 weeks gestation, screened at 4 weeks postnatal age, shows a demarcation line between vascularized and avascular retina. Which stage of retinopathy of prematurity does this represent?
why: Stage 3 shows extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation beyond the ridge, not a flat line
Stage 2 shows an elevated ridge, not a flat demarcation line
Correct — a flat line defines Stage 1
Stage 4 shows partial retinal detachment
exp: ROP staging progresses by the appearance of the vascular-avascular junction: Stage 1 is a flat demarcation line, Stage 2 is a raised ridge, Stage 3 adds extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation beyond the ridge, Stage 4 is partial retinal detachment, and Stage 5 is total detachment.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A young patient with a history of atopy presents with intense itching, ropy discharge, and cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva. Which condition is most likely?
why: Trachoma causes follicular conjunctivitis with eventual scarring (Arlt's line) and trichiasis, not cobblestone papillae
Correct — giant cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with intense itching and ropy discharge in a young atopic patient is classic for vernal keratoconjunctivitis
Bacterial conjunctivitis causes purulent discharge without cobblestone papillae
Pterygium is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth on the conjunctiva and cornea, unrelated to papillary itching
exp: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a bilateral, recurrent, IgE- and cell-mediated allergic conjunctivitis of young atopic patients (often boys, in warm climates), characterized by giant cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, intense itching, and ropy mucoid discharge. Topical mast cell stabilizers and antihistamines are first line; steroids are reserved for flares.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Chronic anterior uveitis, especially in juvenile idiopathic arthritis, classically causes which corneal complication due to calcium deposition in Bowman's layer?
why: Keratoconus is a primary corneal ectasia unrelated to uveitis or calcium deposition.
Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy is a primary endothelial cell disorder causing corneal oedema, not a uveitis complication.
Corneal arcus is lipid deposition at the corneal periphery, associated with ageing or hyperlipidaemia, not uveitis.
Correct - band keratopathy from chronic ocular inflammation, classically in JIA-associated uveitis.
exp: Band keratopathy - calcium salt deposition in a horizontal band across Bowman's layer in the interpalpebral zone - is a well-recognised long-term complication of chronic anterior uveitis, most classically seen in children with JIA-associated uveitis, which is why routine slit-lamp screening is mandated in JIA follow-up.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: In hypermetropia (hyperopia), the image of a distant object is focused:
opts: In front of the retina, requiring a concave lens
Behind the retina, corrected with a convex lens
Behind the retina, corrected with a cylindrical lens
why: Describes myopia, which is corrected with a concave lens, not hyperopia
Would be emmetropia, not hyperopia
Correct - this is the definition of hyperopia and its standard correction
A cylindrical lens corrects astigmatism, not simple hyperopia
exp: Hypermetropia occurs when the eyeball is axially too short or the refractive power too weak, so the image focuses behind the retina; it is corrected with a convex (plus) lens that converges rays more - the mirror opposite of myopia, where the image falls in front of the retina and is corrected with a concave (minus) lens.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 68-year-old hypertensive man develops sudden, painless, unilateral loss of vision. Fundus examination shows a swollen optic disc, dilated tortuous retinal veins, and diffuse flame-shaped haemorrhages in all four quadrants, described as a blood and thunder appearance. What is the diagnosis?
why: CRAO produces a pale oedematous retina with a cherry-red macular spot, not flame haemorrhages
Correct - this fundus picture is classic for CRVO
Vitreous haemorrhage obscures fundus details with a hazy or absent view, not this distinct pattern
Retinitis pigmentosa shows bone-spicule pigmentation with attenuated arterioles, a chronic not acute presentation
exp: The blood and thunder fundus - disc oedema, venous dilatation and tortuosity, and diffuse flame-shaped haemorrhages in all quadrants - is pathognomonic of central retinal vein occlusion, typically in an elderly hypertensive with vascular risk factors; this contrasts with CRAO's pale oedematous retina and cherry-red spot from arterial occlusion.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Keratometry shows the two principal corneal meridians perpendicular to each other but with unequal curvature. This describes which type of astigmatism?
why: Correct — perpendicular principal meridians define regular astigmatism.
Irregular astigmatism means the meridians are not perpendicular or curvature varies within a meridian (e.g. keratoconus); needs a rigid contact lens, not spectacles.
Compound myopic astigmatism describes the refractive pattern (both meridians myopic), not the regular/irregular classification asked here.
Simple hypermetropic astigmatism is a specific refractive subtype, not the general regular/irregular category.
exp: Regular astigmatism has principal meridians exactly 90 degrees apart with uniform curvature in each meridian — correctable with a cylindrical lens. Irregular astigmatism (meridians not perpendicular, or curvature varying within a meridian, as in keratoconus or corneal scarring) needs a rigid contact lens since spectacles cannot correct it.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A cherry-red spot at the macula with surrounding retinal pallor/whitening on fundus examination is classically seen in which condition?
why: CRVO shows disc edema, dilated tortuous veins, and diffuse hemorrhages (blood and thunder fundus), not a cherry-red spot
Retinal detachment shows an elevated, folded, grey retina, not a cherry-red spot
AMD shows drusen, geographic atrophy, or choroidal neovascularization, not this acute ischemic sign
Correct
exp: In central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), sudden ischemia causes opacification/whitening of the surrounding retina from edema of the ganglion cell layer, while the thin fovea — nourished directly by the underlying choroidal circulation — stays relatively translucent, producing the classic cherry-red spot against pale retina. CRAO is an ophthalmic emergency with sudden, painless, profound monocular vision loss.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Anterior uveitis presenting with large, greasy mutton-fat keratic precipitates and broad-based posterior synechiae is most characteristic of which category of uveitis?
exp: Mutton-fat keratic precipitates (large, greasy clumps of epithelioid cells and macrophages on the corneal endothelium) with broad-based posterior synechiae point to granulomatous anterior uveitis, classically from TB, sarcoidosis, sympathetic ophthalmia, or Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease. Non-granulomatous uveitis (HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, JIA) instead shows fine, dust-like KPs and thin, easily broken synechiae.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: On retinoscopy in a patient with keratoconus, which characteristic reflex is seen due to the irregular corneal astigmatism?
exp: Keratoconus causes irregular astigmatism, producing a scissoring reflex on retinoscopy. The oil-droplet (Charleux) reflex is a different classic sign of keratoconus but is seen on distant direct ophthalmoscopy, not retinoscopy.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 48-year-old teacher with previously normal distance vision now holds newspapers at arm's length to read comfortably, while her distance vision remains unaffected. What is the underlying optical mechanism, and which lens corrects it?
opts: Reduced axial length of the globe, corrected with a concave lens
Age-related decline in the accommodative power of the lens from reduced ciliary muscle efficiency and lens elasticity, corrected with a convex ("plus") addition lens for near work
Irregular corneal curvature in two meridians, corrected with a cylindrical lens
Increased corneal curvature, corrected with a divergent lens
exp: Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodative amplitude from progressive lens sclerosis and reduced ciliary muscle efficiency — not a refractive error of the resting eye — and typically becomes symptomatic after age 40. It is corrected with a convex near-addition lens, with the required add increasing roughly from +1.0 D around age 40 to about +3.0 D by age 60.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: In axial myopia, where do parallel light rays from a distant object come to focus relative to the retina?
exp: Axial myopia results from an eyeball too long for its refractive power, so the image of a distant object forms anterior to the retina, causing blurred distance vision; it is corrected with a concave (diverging, minus-power) lens that shifts the focal point back onto the retina. Hypermetropia is the reverse, with the focal point falling behind the retina.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: Image described: fluorescein staining under cobalt-blue light shows a branching, tree-like corneal ulcer with terminal bulbs. This dendritic pattern is pathognomonic of keratitis due to which organism?
why: Correct: a dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs is pathognomonic of HSV epithelial keratitis
Acanthamoeba gives a ring infiltrate and radial perineuritis in contact-lens wearers
Pseudomonas causes a rapidly spreading suppurative ulcer, not dendrites
Fusarium gives a dry ulcer with feathery margins and satellite lesions
exp: A dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs, best demonstrated with fluorescein and cobalt-blue light, is the pathognomonic sign of herpes simplex virus (HSV) epithelial keratitis, and topical corticosteroids are contraindicated as they can worsen it into a geographic ulcer.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A farmer presents 5 days after a paddy leaf injury to the eye with pain, photophobia, and a corneal ulcer. Image described: slit-lamp photo shows a corneal ulcer with feathery, filamentous margins and satellite lesions surrounding the main ulcer. Which organism is most likely responsible?
why: Pseudomonas causes a rapidly spreading ulcer with a ground-glass, mucopurulent look
HSV gives a dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs
Acanthamoeba follows contact-lens and water exposure, with a ring infiltrate and severe pain
Correct: Fusarium keratitis after vegetative trauma shows feathery margins and satellite lesions
exp: Vegetative trauma (paddy leaf, thorn, wood) in an agricultural worker followed by a corneal ulcer with feathery, indistinct margins, satellite lesions, and a dry rough surface is the classic picture of fungal keratitis, most commonly caused by Fusarium (and Aspergillus) in India. This contrasts with Pseudomonas ulcers, which are rapidly progressive with a ground-glass, mucopurulent appearance.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: As per Hofstetter's formula for minimum amplitude of accommodation, what is the expected minimum amplitude at age 40 years?
why: 15 minus 0.25 times 40 equals 5 D, correct
7 D corresponds to roughly age 32, not 40
10 D corresponds to roughly age 20
2.5 D corresponds to roughly age 50
exp: Hofstetter's formula (minimum amplitude = 15 minus 0.25 times age in years) predicts the expected accommodative reserve for a given age and is used to anticipate the onset and progression of presbyopia.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: In granulomatous anterior uveitis, iris nodules located specifically at the pupillary margin are termed?
why: Busacca nodules sit on the iris stroma, not the pupillary border
Correct — Koeppe nodules occur at the pupillary margin
'Berlin nodules' is not a recognized ophthalmic finding
'Roth nodules' does not exist — not to be confused with Roth spots, a retinal finding
exp: Granulomatous uveitis produces two classic iris nodule types: Koeppe nodules at the pupillary margin and Busacca nodules on the iris stroma away from the margin; both point toward causes like sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, or VKH disease rather than non-granulomatous uveitis.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 6-year-old boy presents with unilateral leukocoria. Fundus examination shows massive subretinal lipid exudation with telangiectatic retinal vessels, and B-scan shows no calcification. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Retinoblastoma classically shows a calcified intraocular mass on imaging
Persistent fetal vasculature presents at birth with a retrolental fibrovascular stalk, not telangiectasia
Correct — Coats disease is idiopathic retinal telangiectasia with exudative detachment in young boys, mimicking retinoblastoma but without calcification
ROP occurs in preterm, oxygen-exposed infants, not a term 6-year-old
exp: Coats disease is an idiopathic retinal telangiectasia causing exudative retinal detachment in young boys; it is an important leukocoria mimicker of retinoblastoma, and the absence of a calcified mass on B-scan/CT is the key discriminator.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A young woman has a unilateral pupil that reacts poorly to light but constricts slowly and tonically to near effort, with absent knee and ankle jerks. Which condition is this?
why: Argyll Robertson pupil is small and irregular (neurosyphilis), not dilated
Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD) shows paradoxical dilation on the swinging-flashlight test, not a tonic near response
Horner syndrome causes miosis with ptosis, not light-near dissociation
Correct — Holmes-Adie syndrome (tonic pupil plus areflexia) shows light-near dissociation with a slow tonic near response
exp: Holmes-Adie syndrome (tonic pupil plus areflexia) results from ciliary ganglion damage, causing light-near dissociation with a slow, tonic near response; it is benign and more common in young women.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 12-year-old boy presents with bilateral corneal haze, photophobia, and deep stromal vascularization (salmon patch), along with notched teeth and sensorineural deafness. Which congenital infection is responsible for this corneal finding?
why: Correct — interstitial keratitis with salmon patch is a late feature of congenital syphilis, part of Hutchinson's triad
Congenital rubella causes cataract and salt-and-pepper retinopathy, not interstitial keratitis
Congenital toxoplasmosis causes chorioretinitis, not corneal vascularization
Congenital CMV causes chorioretinitis and microcephaly, not this corneal picture
exp: Interstitial keratitis with deep stromal vascularization (salmon patch) is a classic late manifestation of congenital syphilis, part of Hutchinson's triad (interstitial keratitis, notched/Hutchinson teeth, sensorineural deafness), typically presenting between 5 and 20 years of age.

subject: Ophthalmology
q: A 45-year-old woman presents with pain, proptosis, and restricted eye movement but minimal external redness. B-scan ultrasonography shows flattening of the posterior globe with fluid in the sub-Tenon's space, forming a 'T-sign'. What is the diagnosis?
why: Orbital cellulitis shows diffuse fat stranding on imaging with systemic signs of infection, not a T-sign
Thyroid eye disease shows enlarged extraocular muscles with tendon sparing, not a T-sign
Correct — the B-scan 'T-sign' is pathognomonic for posterior scleritis
Cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with multiple cranial nerve palsies, diagnosed on MRI/MRV
exp: Posterior scleritis can lack the obvious redness of anterior scleritis, presenting instead with pain, proptosis, and restricted motility; the B-scan 'T-sign' (fluid outlining the optic nerve in the sub-Tenon's space) is considered pathognomonic.
